title: What Is Zoetrope? — Definition
body:
Cinema is the art and technology of moving pictures on film: precinema toys (zoetrope, praxinoscope), Edison's kinetoscope, the Lumières' cinematograph, silent features, synchronized sound, color processes, widescreen wars, and the gauges — 35mm, 16mm, 8mm, Super 8, 70mm — that carried a century of movies before digital projection.

In the context of this database, the Zoetrope is presented as one cinema record among the cinema and film history family. 1834's slitted drum: paper strips animating inside — the Victorian parlor's animation.

title: Origins and History of Zoetrope
body:
The Zoetrope belongs to the 1834–1890s era and traces to William Horner.

Persistence-of-vision toys (phenakistoscope 1832, zoetrope 1834) played with motion; Marey and Muybridge analyzed it photographically. Edison's kinetoscope (1893) peep-showed films; the Lumière brothers projected to a paying audience in Paris, December 1895 — cinema's birthday. Nickelodeons (1905) democratized it; features and Hollywood's studio system industrialized it. Sound arrived with Vitaphone/Movietone (1927, The Jazz Singer); color with Technicolor. Television's 1950s threat provoked Cinerama, CinemaScope, and 70mm spectacle. Home formats (8mm 1932, Super 8 1965) made family movies; video (VHS) moved cinema into the living room in the 1980s.

Within that longer story, Zoetrope: The 'wheel of life'; the parlor toy's 19th-century peak. The zoetrope is the animation's drum.

title: How Zoetrope Works
body:
Film cameras expose 16–24 still frames per second through a rotating shutter; projectors re-flash each frame (double/triple-bladed shutters hit 48–72 flashes/sec) to defeat flicker. Sound-on-film prints carry an optical soundtrack (variable area/density) beside the image, read by an exciter lamp and photocell; later magnetic stripes and digital data (Dolby Digital, DTS, SDDS) rode between sprockets. Color came via additive (Technicolor's three-strip beam splitter) or subtractive dye processes; widescreen via anamorphic squeeze (CinemaScope) or wide gauges (70mm).

Applied to the Zoetrope (1834–1890s, William Horner): The zoetrope is the animation's drum.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of Zoetrope — Components
body:
Every Zoetrope is an assembly of the cinema and film history family's standard parts:

• Camera movement — Intermittent claw/shuttle advancing film frame by frame.
• Rotating shutter — Exposure timing and flicker control.
• Lens / anamorphic — Spherical or squeezed widescreen optics.
• Film gate — Holds film flat at the aperture.
• Take-up / feed reels — Supply and wind-up; Latham loop protects the gate.
• Projector lamp — Carbon arc, xenon — the light cannon.
• Sound head — Optical or magnetic reader for the soundtrack.
• Sprockets & rollers — Transport without scratching.
• Rewind bench — Hand-cranked inspection and repair station.
• Editing splicer — Cement or tape splices joining shots.

When examining a surviving Zoetrope, identify these parts in order: Camera movement, Rotating shutter, Lens / anamorphic, Film gate, Take-up / feed reels, Projector lamp.

title: Cinema and Film History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of cinema and film history:

•  persistence of vision — The retinal afterimage blending frames into motion (simplified but traditional).
• phi phenomenon — The actual perceptual basis of apparent motion.
• 24 fps — The sound-era standard frame rate.
• silent speed — 16–18 fps of the silent era; wrong speed looks comedic.
• intermittent movement — Stop-start film advance; Geneva/Maltese-cross mechanism.
• Latham loop — Slack loop isolating gate shock from reels.
• anamorphic — Horizontally squeezed photography unsqueezed in projection.
• three-strip Technicolor — Beam-splitter camera exposing three B&W negatives.
• optical soundtrack — Variable-area/density audio printed beside the image.
• 70mm / IMAX — Wide gauges for maximum resolution spectacle.
• Super 8 — 1965 cartridge home format; bigger frame than Standard 8.
• newsreel — Weekly cinema news before television killed it.

title: Zoetrope in Culture
body:
Cinema was the 20th century's dream factory and town square: Saturday matinees, newsreels before the feature, drive-ins under the stars, the grindhouse and the palace. Home movies in 8mm flicker are family memory itself. The projector's clatter is nostalgia's soundtrack; 'the movies' meant a place, not a file.

The Zoetrope carries that cultural charge directly: The zoetrope is the animation's drum.

title: Collecting and Preserving Zoetrope
body:
Projectors: check gates and shutters; xenon lamps are costly. Cameras: run film through before trusting. Film prints: check for vinegar syndrome (sniff); store cool/dry. Home movies: transfer to digital, keep originals. Splicers, rewinds, and editor viewers are cheap and delightful.

For the Zoetrope specifically: 1834's slitted drum: paper strips animating inside — the Victorian parlor's animation.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working Zoetrope with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: Zoetrope Restoration Guide
body:
Clean film path; replace belts. Lubricate projector mechanisms per manual. Never run valuable prints through unknown projectors. Digitize with proper scanners (not point-and-shoot). Store film archival: 40°F/30% RH ideal; never in attics.

Restoration order for a Zoetrope: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical cinema record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: Zoetrope — Frame-rate and runtime calculator (Runnable Python)
body:
Computes footage, runtime, and projection flash rates across film gauges — the numbers projectionists lived by.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Zoetrope so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Film gauge math: feet, frames, runtime (public-domain formulas)
GAUGES = {
    "35mm (4-perf)": {"frames_per_foot": 16, "fps": 24},
    "16mm": {"frames_per_foot": 40, "fps": 24},
    "8mm": {"frames_per_foot": 80, "fps": 18},
    "Super 8": {"frames_per_foot": 72, "fps": 18},
    "70mm (5-perf)": {"frames_per_foot": 12.8, "fps": 24},
}
for name, g in GAUGES.items():
    feet_per_min = g["fps"] * 60 / g["frames_per_foot"]
    print(f"{name:18s}: {feet_per_min:5.1f} ft/min  |  2000ft reel = "
          f"{2000/feet_per_min:.0f} min")

# Flicker: 3-blade shutter flashes each frame 3x
fps = 24
print(f"\n{fps}fps x 3-blade shutter = {fps*3} flashes/sec (above flicker fusion)")
